def: Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia (NH3) classified as primary, secondary or tertiary based on how many hydrogen atoms of NH3 are replaced by alkyl/aryl groups.
points: Primary amine (1 degree): one H of NH3 replaced by an alkyl/aryl group, general formula R-NH2.
Secondary amine (2 degree): two H atoms replaced, general formula R-NH-R'.
Tertiary amine (3 degree): all three H atoms replaced, general formula R-N(R')(R'').
This classification is different from alcohols: it is based on number of carbon groups on nitrogen, not on the carbon bearing the group.
Amines can be aliphatic (alkyl groups) or aromatic (at least one aryl group directly on nitrogen, like aniline).
IUPAC names use suffix '-amine', e.g. CH3NH2 is methanamine; common names add 'amine' to alkyl group name, e.g. methylamine.
formula: Primary: R-NH2     Secondary: R-NH-R'     Tertiary: R-N(R')(R'')

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Ammonia NH3"] --> B["Replace 1 H - Primary amine"]
  A --> C["Replace 2 H - Secondary amine"]
  A --> D["Replace 3 H - Tertiary amine"]

example: CH3NH2 is a primary amine (methanamine), (CH3)2NH is secondary (N-methylmethanamine), (CH3)3N is tertiary (N,N-dimethylmethanamine).
tip: Identify degree by counting carbon groups attached to N (not to carbon) - this is the most common point students confuse with alcohols.

def: Amines can be prepared by reduction of various nitrogen-containing compounds like nitro compounds, nitriles and amides, or by reactions like Gabriel phthalimide synthesis.
points: Reduction of nitro compounds (R-NO2) using H2/catalyst or Sn/HCl gives primary amines.
Reduction of nitriles (R-CN) using H2/catalyst or LiAlH4 gives primary amines.
Reduction of amides (R-CONH2) using LiAlH4 gives primary amines.
Ammonolysis of alkyl halides: R-X + excess NH3 gives primary amine (but tends to give mixture of 1,2,3-amine due to further alkylation).
Gabriel phthalimide synthesis gives pure primary amines without over-alkylation, using phthalimide, KOH, then alkyl halide, followed by hydrolysis.
Hoffmann bromamide degradation: amide + Br2/NaOH gives primary amine with one carbon LESS than the starting amide.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Nitro compound or nitrile or amide"] --> B["Reduction with H2/catalyst or LiAlH4"]
  B --> C["Primary amine R-NH2"]
  D["Phthalimide + KOH + R-X"] --> E["Hydrolysis"]
  E --> C

example: CH3CONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH --Hoffmann--> CH3NH2 (methanamine, one carbon less than acetamide's 2 carbons).
tip: Remember Gabriel synthesis gives ONLY pure primary amine (no over-alkylation) and Hoffmann degradation reduces carbon count by one - both are frequently asked distinctly.

def: Amines are basic because the nitrogen atom has a lone pair of electrons that can accept a proton (H+), and their basic strength depends on availability of this lone pair.
points: In aqueous solution, basicity order for aliphatic amines is generally: secondary > primary > tertiary (due to combined effect of +I effect, steric hindrance and solvation of the resulting cation).
+I (electron donating) effect of alkyl groups increases electron density on N, increasing basicity.
Too many bulky alkyl groups (as in tertiary amine) cause steric hindrance, making it harder for the cation formed to be solvated/stabilised in water, lowering basicity.
Aromatic amines (like aniline) are much weaker bases than aliphatic amines because the lone pair on N is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, making it less available to accept H+.
Electron-withdrawing groups on the aromatic ring (like -NO2) further decrease basicity of aryl amines; electron-donating groups (-CH3, -OCH3) increase it.
Overall general order: aliphatic amines > ammonia > aromatic amines (aniline) in basicity.
formula: Aqueous basicity order: secondary > primary > tertiary (aliphatic); aliphatic amine > aniline

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Amine basicity depends on lone pair availability"] --> B["Alkyl groups - +I effect increases basicity"]
  A --> C["Bulky groups - steric hindrance decreases basicity"]
  A --> D["Aryl group - lone pair delocalised, decreases basicity"]

example: Aniline (C6H5NH2) is a weaker base than methylamine (CH3NH2) because aniline's nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance.
tip: Explain basicity using BOTH electronic (+I, resonance) and steric factors - a one-sided explanation loses marks in a 'why' question.

def: Hinsberg test distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary amines using benzenesulphonyl chloride, based on differences in solubility and reactivity of the products formed.
points: Benzenesulphonyl chloride (C6H5SO2Cl, Hinsberg reagent) is added to the amine along with KOH.
Primary amine forms N-alkylbenzenesulphonamide, which has an acidic N-H and dissolves in KOH (soluble in alkali) due to formation of a soluble salt.
Secondary amine forms N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide, which has NO acidic N-H left (both H replaced), so it is insoluble in KOH.
Tertiary amine does not react with benzenesulphonyl chloride at all (no N-H to replace), so it remains unreacted/insoluble, simply separates as oily layer.
This test is used as a simple chemical method to identify and separate the three types of amines in a mixture.
After separating, acidifying the KOH-soluble primary amine product regenerates the free primary amine (precipitate reappears).
formula: R-NH2 + C6H5SO2Cl -> R-NH-SO2-C6H5 (soluble in KOH) + HCl

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Add Hinsberg reagent + KOH"] --> B["Primary amine - soluble product in KOH"]
  A --> C["Secondary amine - insoluble product, no acidic H left"]
  A --> D["Tertiary amine - no reaction at all"]

example: CH3NH2 + C6H5SO2Cl gives CH3NHSO2C6H5 which dissolves in KOH (due to acidic N-H), confirming it is a primary amine.
tip: Explain WHY secondary amide product is insoluble (no acidic N-H left) - just stating solubility without the reason loses marks.

def: The carbylamine (isocyanide) reaction is a specific test for primary amines, where the amine reacts with chloroform and alcoholic KOH to give a foul-smelling isocyanide.
points: Only primary amines (aliphatic or aromatic) give this test; secondary and tertiary amines do NOT react.
Primary amine + chloroform (CHCl3) + alcoholic KOH, on heating, gives an isocyanide (carbylamine) and KCl plus water.
The isocyanide formed has a characteristic very unpleasant/foul smell, which confirms the test.
This test is useful to distinguish primary amines from secondary and tertiary amines simply by smell after heating.
Also called isocyanide test since the product R-NC is an isocyanide (carbylamine is the old/common name).
Works for both aliphatic amines (R-NH2) and aromatic amines (Ar-NH2) since both have the required N-H2 group.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Primary amine R-NH2"] --> B["+ CHCl3 + alcoholic KOH, heat"]
  B --> C["Isocyanide R-NC - foul smell"]
  C --> D["Confirms primary amine"]

example: C6H5NH2 (aniline) + CHCl3 + alcoholic KOH gives C6H5NC (phenyl isocyanide) with a foul smell, confirming aniline is a primary amine.
tip: State explicitly that only primary amines give this positive test, and mention 'foul smell' as the observable result - this is the expected keyword.

def: Diazonium salts are compounds of the general formula Ar-N2+X-, formed by reacting primary aromatic amines with nitrous acid at low temperature, and are very reactive intermediates in organic synthesis.
points: Formed by diazotisation: aromatic primary amine + NaNO2 + dilute HCl (or H2SO4) at low temperature (0-5 degree C).
Low temperature is essential because diazonium salts are unstable and decompose above 5 degree C (especially in water, giving phenol).
Diazonium salts undergo substitution reactions where N2 gas is released and replaced by another group, e.g. -OH (water), -Cl (HCl), -CN (KCN/CuCN, Sandmeyer reaction).
Coupling reactions: diazonium salt reacts with phenol or aniline (in alkaline/weakly acidic medium) to form brightly coloured azo compounds (azo dyes) without losing nitrogen.
Diazonium salts are very important intermediates to introduce various functional groups onto a benzene ring that are otherwise hard to add directly.
Reduction of diazonium salt with H3PO2/H2O (or ethanol) replaces N2+ with H, useful to remove the amino group entirely from the ring.
formula: Ar-NH2 + NaNO2 + HCl --(273-278 K)--> Ar-N2+Cl- + NaCl + 2H2O

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Aromatic primary amine"] --> B["NaNO2 + HCl, 0-5 degree C"]
  B --> C["Diazonium salt Ar-N2+Cl-"]
  C --> D["Substitution - replace N2 with OH, Cl, CN"]
  C --> E["Coupling - azo dye with phenol or aniline"]

example: Aniline + NaNO2 + HCl at 0-5 degree C gives benzenediazonium chloride, which couples with phenol in alkaline medium to form a bright orange-red azo dye.
tip: Always mention the low temperature condition (0-5 degree C) for diazotisation - omitting this is a very common mark-losing mistake.
